title: Predicting Species Splits: A Challenging Fine-Grained Benchmark for Category Discovery
claim: Fine-grained categories can split into new ones over time; telling which known category should split requires subtle visual and geographic cues.
layout: 3 columns: left example, center world map, right example; zoom-in connectors
description: The figure has three columns. At left, titled American Robin, are two bird photos in teal frames, with the text 'Q: Split into new species? A: No' in red. At right, titled Naumann's Thrush, are two thrush photos in blue and orange frames. Below them is 'Q: Split into new species? A: Yes, Dusky & Naumann's Thrush', in colored text, and a line 'black chevrons vs red chevrons'. The center shows a world map with a heatmap of image density in purple, orange and pink. Teal and yellow circles on the map (North America, East Asia) link by zoom-in lines to regional maps. The regional maps show colored dots for observation locations: teal for the robin, and blue and orange for the two thrushes. The eye goes first to the bird photos and the map.
caption: Real-world visual categories can split over time. Here we illustrate two categories from our PS-SPLIT dataset. The American Robin, which can be found across North America, has not been subject to any taxonomic splits. In contrast, the Dusky Thrush was previously considered to be a subspecies of Naumann’s Thrush, but has subsequently been determined to be a distinct species based on appearance/morphological, geographic, and genetic cues [1]. The world map shows the distribution of images in PS-SPLIT, and locations where the individual birds depicted have been observed are denoted with colored circles in the regional maps.
abstract: Widely used category discovery benchmarks have become increasingly saturated and often fail to reflect real-world discovery settings, making long-term evaluation of new methods difficult. We introduce PS-SPLIT, a large-scale fine-grained benchmark for category discovery, motivated by taxonomic splitting: the real-world process by which what was once considered a single species is found to comprise multiple distinct ones. PS-SPLIT contains 79K globally distributed, high-quality, community-collected bird images spanning 771 species, derived from 257 recent real expert-verified taxonomic splits, with associated geographic metadata and full taxonomic hierarchy. The visual differences between categories arising from real taxonomic splits can be very subtle, often requiring significant human expertise to tell apart, making PS-SPLIT a challenging benchmark which we hope will assist in advancing fine-grained category discovery research. Based on taxonomic splitting, we introduce the task of discovery by category splitting, where the goal is to determine which known categories should be subdivided into new finer-grained subcategories. We adapt four generalized category discovery methods to this setting, evaluate existing methods, and show that there is substantial room for future progress.
